Review Text: Most of the time, while working as a customer service supervisor, we were understaffed. Team members from other departments were supposed to help out during busy periods, but rarely did, which left customers complaining about ques and service quality as there was a rush to get customers out of the store. Service staff got tired of being stuck on register and often complained or regularly called in sick and cancelled shifts at the last minute, making these shifts very difficult to replace. A number of jobs were required of service staff in addition to customer service (for example cleaning, putting stock away, filling drink fridges and confectionery stands) and due to lack of staff these jobs were often left not done. Store managers and other higher up staff would then complain to me and my direct customer service manager, without recognizing that the reason tasks were not completed was due to lack of staff, not incompetence. Customers, particularly cigarette customers and refund customers tended to be difficult. Cigarette customers were often rude and demanding, as were refund customers. Some refund customers claimed to know our refund policy more than myself, who had been working there for over 7 years, and demanded free products, when this was not allowed.

These factors played a significant role in my decision to leave NEXTDC. While I encountered challenges during my time here, I also recognize that every organization has room for improvement. Firstly, I would encourage NEXTDC to consider enhancing communication and transparency within the company. Clearer communication channels and a more transparent decision-making process can help employees understand the company's direction and feel more engaged Secondly, I would suggest exploring ways to foster a more inclusive and diverse workplace. This could involve initiatives to ensure that all employees, regardless of their roles or schedules, feel valued and included. Lastly, I would recommend evaluating opportunities for professional growth and career advancement within the organization. A structured approach to career development and mentorship programs can go long way in retaining and nurturing talent.

Bupa’s culture is characterised by structural ambiguity, operational self‑protection, and a consistent reluctance to support or empower its clinical workforce. Bupa prioritises maintaining its relationship with Defence and protecting its own organisational interests over advocating for its contracted employees. Bupa operates on deliberate operational vagueness. Position descriptions, contractual clauses, reporting lines, and role expectations are kept intentionally broad, allowing Bupa to shift responsibilities, avoid accountability, and expand duties without consultation or remuneration. Requests for clarification are routinely deflected, minimised, or reframed, and you will risk being labelled as “difficult” or “resistant.” Professional development support is minimal, tightly controlled, and often obstructed, especially when it involves financial investment. Even entitlements explicitly advertised are withheld or negotiated down. Staff you are training will be paid a higher rate!

I worked as a civilian within the Department in a large number of different roles and locations for over 9 years. I found it was highly political environment; you needed to have a large degree of patience due to the complex processes and management structures. There were often large periods of inactivity with brief spurts of panicked rush due to failures of communication or changes in business direction. While the majority of the leadership is either current or former military who are trained in a management style not really suitable for an office environment. However, the biggest issue is the inability to deal constructively with any workplace conflict. I saw long periods of paralysis due to inter-management conflicts, personal grievances or because of competing power structures. Due to Public Service restraints the leadership is unable to permanently deal with issues, while the official dispute resolution system, although well-meaning is not fit for purpose and open for manipulation. Remember many of your experiences and the skills developed in Defence are not readily transferable to other industries/fields. So, once you have been in the Department for longer than a couple of years, you are stuck in the Defence environment for the rest of your working life unless you are willing to make a major career change. In summary, as a civilian you must be highly politically minded, with extremely high interpersonal skills and a large amount of patience to succeed. It is not an environment for those who are technically focused or goal orientated, if you are it can be very frustrating and damaging to your mental health in the long term.

Flexibility reduced significantly, and the working environment became more restrictive, including situations where attending a doctor’s appointment was treated as requiring annual leave. In my experience, the team lacked clear direction, consistent priorities, and role ownership. This was made harder by limited technical leadership to guide data engineering, BI, analytics, governance, or strategy-based work. There was also a strong sense of micromanagement, with too much focus on task tracking and short-term delivery rather than quality outcomes or long-term capability building. I would suggest caution to anyone considering this specific team, as several members, including newer data engineers, left within a short period. The roles may look appealing externally, but the team environment was difficult in practice.

The team consists of eight members, four data engineers and four BI and analytics engineers, yet there is a lack of clear role alignment and ownership across the group. The team reports to three different managers, each with competing objectives and priorities, which creates confusion, conflicting directions, and constant context switching. Management demonstrates limited understanding of prioritization and people management, leading to unrealistic expectations and poor support for team members. There is no defined career path. A Senior Data Engineer was hired and he help upskill the team and introduced best practices around process and data governance. However, leadership discouraged these improvements and directed the role to focus solely on individual deliverables, undermining long-term quality and capability building. Agile practices (sprints, daily stand-ups, etc.) were introduced but used as a micromanagement tool. Performance is judged primarily on burn-down charts.

There are areas for improvement. These include the onboarding process, providing ongoing training, ensuring consistency across stores, career progression and implementing WHS. Recently the company has faced a significant turnover of staff. The introduction of new regional managers has led to a lack of cohesion, as everyone is inexperienced. This situation has placed immense pressure on long-standing staff to maintain stability, while new employees overwhelmed due to the steep learning curve. With limited opportunity for career advancement, as employees are often informed that they are not ready for promotion, but no succession plans are established. Those who may not be suitable for management positions are responsible for training new managers. Often, one staff member is left to oversee an entire store without a meal break, even on weekends. Many employees find themselves staying late after their shifts to finish their work.
